audience: Anyone learning Java backend development, including complete beginners

pages.title: WHAT IS JAVA BACKEND DEVELOPMENT?
pages.objective: Backend development means writing the hidden part of an application that receives requests, applies rules, saves data, and sends results.
pages.layout: Top: simple real-life example. Middle: request journey. Bottom: frontend/backend comparison.

panels.heading: A SIMPLE EXAMPLE
copy: When you place an online order, the screen you see is the frontend.
The backend checks the product, calculates the total, saves the order, and returns an order number.
Java is a popular language for building this backend part.
panels.visual: Draw phone screen on the left and a Java server plus database on the right.

panels.heading: REQUEST JOURNEY
copy: 1. A user clicks a button.
2. The frontend sends a request through the internet.
3. The Java backend checks the request and performs the work.
4. The database stores or returns data.
5. The backend sends a response to the user.
panels.visual: Five boxes: User → Frontend → Java Backend → Database → Response.

panels.heading: MAIN BACKEND JOBS
copy: Accept data safely.
Follow business rules.
Store and read information.
Protect private data.
Handle errors and stay available.

pages.flowchart: User action → HTTP request → Controller → Service → Database → JSON response.
important: The backend is not normally visible, but it does most of the application's work.
A database stores information; Java code decides what should happen.
summary: Frontend shows; backend works.
Java backend connects user requests with business rules and data.
interview_checks: Explain what happens after a user clicks 'Place Order'.

pages.title: INSTALL JAVA + RUN YOUR FIRST PROGRAM
pages.objective: A Java program is text written in a .java file. The JDK gives us the tools needed to compile and run it.
pages.layout: Top: setup checklist. Middle: Hello World code. Bottom: compile and run flow.

panels.heading: WHAT YOU NEED
copy: Install a supported JDK such as Java 17 or Java 21.
Use an editor or IDE such as IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, or VS Code.
Check installation with java --version and javac --version.
Create a file named Hello.java.
panels.visual: Checklist with JDK, IDE, terminal, source file.

panels.heading: UNDERSTAND THE PROGRAM
copy: class Hello creates a class named Hello.
main is the starting method of a simple Java program.
System.out.println prints text on the screen.
Java names and uppercase/lowercase letters must match exactly.
panels.visual: Arrows from each line of code to its plain meaning.

panels.heading: COMPILE AND RUN
copy: javac Hello.java checks the code and creates Hello.class.
java Hello asks the Java runtime to execute the compiled class.
A compiler error means the code must be corrected before it can run.

pages.flowchart: Hello.java → javac Hello.java → Hello.class → java Hello → Hello, Java!
important: The public class name and file name should match.
Run java Hello, not java Hello.class.
summary: Write source code, compile it, then run it.
main is the starting point of this example.
interview_checks: What is the difference between javac and java?

pages.title: JDK vs JRE vs JVM
pages.objective: JDK, JRE, and JVM are three connected parts that help us build and run Java programs.
pages.layout: Reference-style three-column comparison table with a small flow below.

panels.heading: EASY COMPARISON
copy: JDK — Java Development Kit. It contains tools for writing, compiling, and running Java programs.
JRE — Java Runtime Environment. It means the runtime libraries and JVM needed to run Java code.
JVM — Java Virtual Machine. It reads Java bytecode and runs it on the computer.
Modern Java usually provides a complete JDK; custom runtimes can also be created.
panels.visual: Three columns: Part | Full form | Main job | Used by.

panels.heading: HOW THEY WORK TOGETHER
copy: The compiler javac changes source code into bytecode.
Bytecode is stored in a .class file.
The JVM changes bytecode into instructions the computer can execute.
A JVM is made for a particular operating system, but Java bytecode is portable.

pages.flowchart: Program.java → JDK compiler → Program.class bytecode → JVM → computer output.
important: JDK is used to develop; JVM is used to execute.
Bytecode is the reason the same Java program can run on different systems with a suitable JVM.
summary: JDK builds Java programs.
JVM runs Java bytecode.
interview_checks: Why is Java called platform-independent?

pages.title: STRUCTURE OF A JAVA PROGRAM
pages.objective: A Java program is organized using packages, imports, classes, fields, methods, and statements.
pages.layout: Large labeled code example on left; meaning table on right.

panels.heading: MAIN PARTS
copy: package tells where the class belongs.
import lets us use a class from another package by its short name.
class is a blueprint that groups data and behavior.
field stores data inside an object.
method performs a task.
statement is one instruction and normally ends with a semicolon.
panels.visual: Label each part on the code example with colored arrows.

panels.heading: NAMING STYLE
copy: Class names use PascalCase: OrderService.
Methods and variables use camelCase: calculateTotal.
Constants normally use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE: MAX_SIZE.
Good names explain purpose better than short names like x or data1.

pages.flowchart: Package contains classes → class contains fields and methods → method contains statements.
important: Java code is read from top-level classes, but program work happens inside methods.
Braces { } group code; indentation makes the groups easy to see.
summary: A class groups related data and actions.
Clear structure and names make code easy to understand.
interview_checks: Name the field and method in the Product example.

pages.title: VARIABLES + DATA TYPES
pages.objective: A variable is a named place that holds a value. Its data type tells Java what kind of value it may hold.
pages.layout: Top definition and boxes. Middle primitive table. Bottom reference example.

panels.heading: VARIABLE PARTS
copy: Declaration: int age; tells Java the name and type.
Assignment: age = 25; puts a value into the variable.
Initialization: int age = 25; does both at once.
A variable can change unless it is declared final.
panels.visual: Draw a labeled box: type | name | value.

panels.heading: 8 PRIMITIVE TYPES
copy: Whole numbers: byte, short, int, long.
Decimal numbers: float, double.
Single character: char.
True or false: boolean.
Primitives directly represent simple values.
panels.visual: Table Type | Example | Simple use.

panels.heading: REFERENCE TYPES
copy: String, arrays, and objects are reference types.
A reference points to an object rather than directly containing the whole object.
null means the reference currently points to no object.

pages.flowchart: Choose meaning → choose suitable type → give clear name → assign value.
important: Use long suffix L and float suffix F when needed.
For money, BigDecimal is safer than double because decimal values must be exact.
summary: A variable has a type, name, and value.
Primitive and reference types store different kinds of information.
interview_checks: Which type would you choose for age, name, and a yes/no answer?

pages.title: OPERATORS IN JAVA
pages.objective: An operator is a symbol that tells Java to calculate, compare, assign, or check values.
pages.layout: Reference-style rows: operator group, symbols, example, result.

panels.heading: OPERATOR GROUPS
copy: Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, % perform calculations.
Assignment: =, +=, -= store or update a value.
Comparison: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <= produce true or false.
Logical: && means AND, || means OR, ! means NOT.
Increment/decrement: ++ and -- add or remove one.
panels.visual: Table Group | Symbols | Example | Result.

panels.heading: ORDER OF WORK
copy: Parentheses run first and make the intention clear.
Multiplication/division normally happen before addition/subtraction.
Short-circuit AND stops when the left side is false.
Short-circuit OR stops when the left side is true.

pages.flowchart: Values → operator → result; comparison result → boolean true/false.
important: Use .equals() to compare String values; == compares object references.
Add parentheses when an expression may be hard to read.
summary: Operators work with values.
Comparison and logical operators help make decisions.
interview_checks: What is the result of 10 + 5 * 2, and why?

pages.title: TYPE CASTING + USER INPUT
pages.objective: Type casting changes a value from one type to another. Input lets a program receive a value from a user or another source.
pages.layout: Left: widening/narrowing arrows. Right: Scanner example and safety notes.

panels.heading: TYPE CASTING
copy: Widening conversion moves a smaller type to a larger compatible type automatically: int to long.
Narrowing conversion moves a larger type to a smaller type and needs an explicit cast.
Narrowing can lose decimal parts or overflow the target range.
Casting does not turn unrelated objects into each other.
panels.visual: Small-to-large green arrow; large-to-small orange warning arrow.

panels.heading: READING INPUT
copy: Scanner can read values from the console in a beginner program.
nextLine reads a line of text; nextInt reads an integer.
Real web applications receive input from HTTP requests instead of the console.
All outside input must be checked before it is trusted.

pages.flowchart: Outside value → read → convert if needed → validate → use.
important: A cast can lose information; use it only when the allowed range is known.
Input validation prevents wrong values from entering the program.
summary: Widening is usually safe; narrowing may lose data.
Read input, then validate it.
interview_checks: Why does converting double 19.95 to int produce 19?

pages.title: IF, ELSE + SWITCH
pages.objective: Conditional statements let a program choose different work based on a true or false condition.
pages.layout: Top if/else flowchart. Middle examples. Bottom switch table.

panels.heading: IF / ELSE
copy: if runs a block when its condition is true.
else if checks another condition when earlier ones were false.
else runs when no earlier condition matched.
Conditions should be clear and should not perform hidden work.
panels.visual: Decision diamond: condition? true path / false path.

panels.heading: SWITCH
copy: switch compares one value with several possible cases.
Arrow-style cases avoid accidental fall-through.
A default case handles values not listed.
Use if for ranges/complex conditions and switch for clear named choices.

pages.flowchart: Start → check condition → choose one path → continue after decision.
important: Use braces even for short blocks; they prevent mistakes during later changes.
Keep the normal path simple by rejecting invalid input early.
summary: if chooses by a condition.
switch chooses among known values.
interview_checks: When is switch clearer than a long if/else chain?

pages.title: LOOPS: FOR, WHILE + DO-WHILE
pages.objective: A loop repeats a block of code until a condition says it should stop.
pages.layout: Three-column comparison with one flow diagram and loop-control notes.

panels.heading: THREE LOOPS
copy: for is useful when the number of repetitions is known.
enhanced for reads each item from an array or collection.
while checks the condition before every repetition.
do-while runs once before checking its condition.
panels.visual: Columns Loop | Best use | Small example.

panels.heading: LOOP CONTROL
copy: break immediately leaves the loop.
continue skips the rest of the current repetition.
A loop needs progress toward stopping, or it may run forever.
Avoid changing a normal collection while using an enhanced for loop over it.

pages.flowchart: Initialize → check condition → run body → update → check again → finish.
important: An off-by-one error repeats one time too many or too few.
Use meaningful loop names and small loop bodies.
summary: Loops repeat work.
The condition and update decide when a loop stops.
interview_checks: What is the difference between while and do-while?

pages.title: ARRAYS
pages.objective: An array stores a fixed number of values of the same type in numbered positions.
pages.layout: Top array drawing with indexes. Middle operations. Bottom 1D/2D comparison.

panels.heading: HOW AN ARRAY WORKS
copy: The first position has index 0.
An array of length 5 has indexes 0 through 4.
length gives the number of positions.
Reading an index outside the range causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
panels.visual: Five boxes labeled values with indexes 0,1,2,3,4 below.

panels.heading: CREATE AND USE
copy: The size is fixed when the array is created.
Primitive array positions receive default primitive values.
Object array positions start as null.
Use ArrayList when the number of items must easily grow or shrink.

pages.flowchart: Create size → fill positions → read/update by index → loop through values.
important: Array length is scores.length, not scores.length().
A two-dimensional array is an array whose elements are arrays.
summary: Arrays store same-type values in fixed positions.
Array indexes start at zero.
interview_checks: What are the valid indexes of an array with length 4?

pages.title: METHODS + PARAMETERS
pages.objective: A method is a named block of code that performs one task and can be used again.
pages.layout: Large method anatomy with labels; call flow beneath.

panels.heading: METHOD PARTS
copy: Access modifier controls where it can be called.
Return type tells what value comes back; void means no value.
Method name should describe the action.
Parameters are input names in the method definition.
Arguments are actual values given when calling it.
panels.visual: Label public, int, add, parameters, body, return.

panels.heading: WHY METHODS HELP
copy: They divide a large problem into small steps.
One tested method can be reused.
A short method is easier to read and change.
Method overloading allows the same name with different parameter lists.

pages.flowchart: Caller gives arguments → method parameters receive copied values → body runs → return value goes to caller.
important: Java passes every argument by value; an object argument copies the reference value.
A method should usually do one clearly named job.
summary: Parameters bring values in; return sends a value out.
Methods organize and reuse logic.
interview_checks: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?

pages.title: CLASS vs OBJECT
pages.objective: A class is a blueprint. An object is one real instance created from that blueprint.
pages.layout: Reference-style comparison table and two-object memory drawing.

panels.heading: EASY COMPARISON
copy: Class: describes fields and methods shared by a kind of thing.
Object: has its own field values and can use the class methods.
One class can create many objects.
The new keyword normally creates an object and calls a constructor.
panels.visual: Two columns Class | Object with definition, creation, memory, example.

panels.heading: STATE + BEHAVIOR
copy: State means the current data, such as account balance.
Behavior means actions, such as deposit or withdraw.
Each BankAccount object can have a different balance.
Methods protect how state is changed.

pages.flowchart: Class blueprint → new → object 1 and object 2, each with separate field values.
important: A variable such as redCar stores a reference to the object.
Two references can point to the same object.
summary: Class describes; object exists.
Objects combine data and actions.
interview_checks: Can one class create many objects? Give an example.

pages.title: CONSTRUCTORS, this + static
pages.objective: A constructor prepares a new object. this means the current object. static belongs to the class rather than one object.
pages.layout: Three horizontal parts with object creation flow.

panels.heading: CONSTRUCTOR
copy: A constructor has the same name as the class and no return type.
It runs when new creates an object.
It should place the object in a valid starting state.
Constructors can be overloaded with different parameter lists.
panels.visual: new Product(...) arrow into constructor then ready object.

panels.heading: this
copy: this.name means the name field of the current object.
It is useful when a parameter and field have the same name.
this(...) calls another constructor and must be the first constructor statement.

panels.heading: static
copy: A static field is shared by all objects of the class.
A static method can be called using the class name.
A static method cannot directly use instance fields because no current object is selected.

pages.flowchart: new Product("Book") → constructor validates/sets fields → object is ready; shared count increases.
important: Java supplies a no-argument default constructor only when no constructor is written.
Do not use static as a replacement for proper objects and dependencies.
summary: Constructor creates a valid starting object.
this is current object; static is class-level.
interview_checks: Why is this.name = name used in a constructor?

pages.title: ACCESS MODIFIERS + PACKAGES
pages.objective: Access modifiers control where a class member can be used. Packages group related classes and avoid name conflicts.
pages.layout: Large four-row visibility table plus package tree.

panels.heading: VISIBILITY
copy: private: only inside the same class.
no modifier (package-private): classes in the same package.
protected: same package and qualifying subclasses.
public: available from other packages when the class is accessible.
panels.visual: Table Modifier | Same class | Same package | Subclass | Other package.

panels.heading: PACKAGES
copy: A package name usually follows a reversed internet-domain style: com.example.shop.
The folder structure normally follows the package name.
import gives a short way to refer to a class from another package.
java.lang classes such as String are imported automatically.

pages.flowchart: Application → feature package → related classes; public API outside, private details inside.
important: Choose the smallest visibility that the design needs.
private data is accessed through meaningful methods, not automatically through a setter for every field.
summary: Modifiers protect access.
Packages organize related code.
interview_checks: What is the difference between private and public?

pages.title: OOP CONCEPTS — ONE EASY VIEW
pages.objective: Object-oriented programming organizes software around objects that contain data and actions.
pages.layout: Reference-style five-row grid with definition, small example, and benefit.

panels.heading: 1. ENCAPSULATION
copy: Keep data and the methods that safely change it together.
Example: BankAccount keeps balance private and provides deposit().
Benefit: protects valid data.
panels.visual: Row arrow → Data protection.

panels.heading: 2. ABSTRACTION
copy: Show what an object can do and hide unnecessary internal steps.
Example: pay() hides payment-provider details.
Benefit: simpler use.
panels.visual: Row arrow → Hides complexity.

panels.heading: 3. INHERITANCE
copy: A child class receives accessible behavior from a parent class.
Example: Dog extends Animal.
Benefit: shared behavior when there is a true IS-A relation.
panels.visual: Animal → Dog.

panels.heading: 4. POLYMORPHISM
copy: The same method call can behave differently for different objects.
Example: shape.draw() works for Circle and Rectangle.
Benefit: flexible code.
panels.visual: Shape branches to Circle/Rectangle.

panels.heading: 5. ASSOCIATION
copy: Objects can use or contain other objects.
Example: Order has Customer and LineItem objects.
Benefit: models relationships.

pages.flowchart: Real thing → class model → data + methods → collaborating objects.
important: OOP is not only writing classes; it is placing responsibilities in clear objects.
Prefer simple object relationships over deep inheritance trees.
summary: OOP groups state and behavior.
Four main ideas are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism.
interview_checks: Explain each OOP concept using one simple example.

pages.title: ENCAPSULATION + DATA HIDING
pages.objective: Encapsulation means keeping an object's data private and allowing it to change only through safe methods.
pages.layout: Top definition. Middle bad/good comparison. Bottom account example.

panels.heading: WHY HIDE DATA?
copy: Public fields can be changed to any value from anywhere.
Private fields stop outside code from changing data directly.
Public methods can check a value before changing the field.
This keeps the object in a valid state.
panels.visual: Open box with unsafe arrows versus protected box with one checked entrance.

panels.heading: GETTERS AND SETTERS
copy: A getter returns a value when callers need to read it.
A setter changes a value, but it should validate the new value.
Not every field needs both a getter and setter.
A meaningful method such as withdraw(amount) is clearer than setBalance(value).

pages.flowchart: Caller → public method → validation → private field changes safely.
important: Encapsulation is more than private fields; it protects rules.
Expose actions the object supports, not all internal details.
summary: Private data + safe methods = encapsulation.
The object protects its own valid state.
interview_checks: Why is withdraw(amount) better than a public balance field?

pages.title: INHERITANCE + IS-A RELATIONSHIP
pages.objective: Inheritance lets one class receive behavior from another class when the child is truly a type of the parent.
pages.layout: Parent/child diagram, syntax, and use/do-not-use comparison.

panels.heading: PARENT AND CHILD
copy: The parent or superclass contains common behavior.
The child or subclass uses extends and may add or change behavior.
A Dog IS-A Animal, so the relationship can make sense.
Constructors are not inherited, but a child constructor can call super(...).
panels.visual: Animal top box; Dog and Cat child boxes.

panels.heading: WHEN TO USE
copy: Use inheritance when every child can safely be used wherever the parent is expected.
Do not use inheritance only to copy some code.
A Car is not an Engine; a Car HAS-A Engine, so composition is better.
Java classes can extend only one class.

pages.flowchart: General parent → common behavior → specialized child adds behavior.
important: private parent fields are not directly accessible in the child.
Favor composition when there is no clear IS-A relationship.
summary: Inheritance shares behavior through an IS-A relation.
A child should respect the parent's promise.
interview_checks: Is Car extends Engine a good design? Why or why not?

pages.title: POLYMORPHISM: OVERLOADING vs OVERRIDING
pages.objective: Polymorphism means 'many forms': one name or contract can work in more than one way.
pages.layout: Reference-style two-column comparison and runtime object diagram.

panels.heading: METHOD OVERLOADING
copy: Same method name, different parameter list.
Usually written in the same class.
The compiler selects the method using the argument types.
Return type alone cannot create a valid overload.
panels.visual: Compile-time label with two add methods.

panels.heading: METHOD OVERRIDING
copy: A child class gives a new implementation of an inherited method.
Name and parameter list match the parent method.
@Override lets the compiler check our intention.
The real object type chooses the method while the program runs.
panels.visual: Animal reference points to Dog object; sound() prints Woof.

panels.heading: WHY IT HELPS
copy: Code can use a general type such as PaymentMethod.
Different objects perform pay() in their own way.
The caller does not need a large if/else for every concrete type.

code:
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; }

Animal animal = new Dog();
animal.sound(); // Dog version runs
pages.flowchart: General reference → actual object → overridden method runs.
important: Overloading is chosen at compile time; overriding is chosen at runtime.
Use @Override whenever a method is intended to override.
summary: Overloading changes parameters.
Overriding changes inherited behavior.
interview_checks: Give one difference between overloading and overriding.

pages.title: ABSTRACT CLASS vs INTERFACE
pages.objective: An abstract class is an incomplete base class. An interface is a contract that tells what a class can do.
pages.layout: Reference-matched three-column table with 10 easy rows and a choice guide.

panels.heading: FEATURE COMPARISON
copy: Definition — abstract class: base class that cannot be created directly; interface: contract/capability implemented by classes.
Keyword — abstract class uses abstract; interface uses interface.
Methods — abstract class may have abstract and normal methods; interface may have abstract, default, static, and private methods.
Variables — abstract class may have instance fields; interface fields are constants (public static final).
Constructor — abstract class can have constructors; interface cannot.
Inheritance — extend one class; implement multiple interfaces.
Access — class members can use different access levels; interface abstract methods are public.
Use — shared state/base behavior versus a common capability.
Example — Animal base class versus Drawable contract.
Modern Java — interfaces can also contain useful default helper behavior.
panels.visual: Columns Feature | Abstract Class | Interface; ten numbered rows.

panels.heading: SIMPLE CHOICE
copy: Need shared fields and base setup? Choose an abstract class.
Need one class to promise several abilities? Choose interfaces.
Need only to reuse a helper? First consider a separate helper object (composition).

pages.flowchart: Shared base state? → Abstract class. Common ability/multiple roles? → Interface.
important: A class can extend one class and implement many interfaces.
Since Java 8 interfaces may have default/static methods; since Java 9 they may have private helpers.
summary: Abstract class = shared base.
Interface = common contract or ability.
interview_checks: When would you choose an interface instead of an abstract class?

pages.title: Object CLASS + equals + hashCode
pages.objective: Object is the top parent of Java classes. Its common methods help compare, describe, and identify objects.
pages.layout: Method table and two-object equality drawing.

panels.heading: COMMON Object METHODS
copy: toString() returns a text description useful for logs and debugging.
equals() answers whether two objects should be treated as logically equal.
hashCode() gives a number used by hash collections.
getClass() returns the object's runtime class.
panels.visual: Table Method | Easy meaning | Example use.

panels.heading: == vs equals
copy: == compares primitive values directly.
For objects, == asks whether two references point to the same object.
equals asks whether objects represent the same logical value when implemented that way.
String overrides equals, so use it for String value comparison.

panels.heading: THE RULE
copy: If two objects are equal, they must have the same hash code.
Override equals and hashCode together.
Do not change equality fields while an object is inside HashSet or used as a HashMap key.

pages.flowchart: Compare references? → ==. Compare object meaning? → equals → matching hashCode rule.
important: toString should never reveal passwords or secret data.
Records automatically create useful equals, hashCode, and toString methods.
summary: == checks identity for objects; equals checks logical value.
Equal objects need equal hash codes.
interview_checks: Why should equals and hashCode be overridden together?

pages.title: STRING, STRINGBUILDER + STRING POOL
pages.objective: String represents text. String objects are immutable, meaning their text cannot be changed after creation.
pages.layout: Top string pool drawing. Middle method examples. Bottom comparison table.

panels.heading: STRING IMMUTABILITY
copy: A String operation returns a new String instead of changing the old one.
Immutability makes String safe to share and suitable as a map key.
String literals with the same text can share one object in the string pool.
new String(...) normally creates a separate object.
panels.visual: Two literal references point to one pooled 'Java'; new String points outside.

panels.heading: USEFUL METHODS
copy: length gives character count.
equals compares text; equalsIgnoreCase ignores letter case.
substring takes part of the text.
trim/strip removes surrounding whitespace.
split separates text into parts.

panels.heading: BUILDING TEXT
copy: Repeated + inside a loop can create many temporary String objects.
StringBuilder is mutable and efficient for building text on one thread.
StringBuffer is synchronized and is less commonly needed.

pages.flowchart: Original String → operation → new String; StringBuilder → many appends → final String.
important: Use equals, not ==, for String content.
A String can be empty ("") or null; they are different.
summary: String is immutable text.
StringBuilder is useful for repeated text building.
interview_checks: Why does name.toUpperCase() not change the original String?

pages.title: WRAPPER CLASSES, ENUMS + RECORDS
pages.objective: Wrapper classes turn primitive values into objects; enums define fixed choices; records define small data carriers.
pages.layout: Three reference-style rows with definition, example, and use.

panels.heading: WRAPPER CLASSES
copy: Integer wraps int, Long wraps long, Double wraps double, and Boolean wraps boolean.
Generics and collections use objects, so List<Integer> is used instead of List<int>.
Autoboxing converts primitive to wrapper; unboxing converts back.
A wrapper may be null, which can cause a problem during unboxing.
panels.visual: int 5 ↔ Integer object.

panels.heading: ENUM
copy: An enum lists a fixed set of named values.
It is safer than passing random text for a known choice.
Enums may contain fields, constructors, and methods.
Example states: NEW, PAID, SHIPPED.

panels.heading: RECORD
copy: A record is a short way to create a data-focused class.
It creates a constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString.
Its fields cannot be reassigned, but an object stored inside can still be mutable.

pages.flowchart: Simple number → wrapper when object is needed; fixed choices → enum; small data result → record.
important: Compare enum values with ==.
Do not use a wrapper as a field when a primitive clearly cannot be absent.
summary: Wrappers provide object forms of primitives.
Enums name fixed choices; records carry data concisely.
interview_checks: Why does List<int> not work, but List<Integer> does?

pages.title: EXCEPTIONS + try-catch-finally
pages.objective: An exception is an object that tells us something unexpected stopped the normal flow of a program.
pages.layout: Throwable tree on top; try/catch flow and good practices below.

panels.heading: EXCEPTION FAMILY
copy: Throwable is the top type.
Error usually represents a serious JVM/system problem an application does not normally handle.
Exception represents problems application code may report or handle.
RuntimeException is unchecked; other common Exception types are checked by the compiler.
panels.visual: Tree Throwable → Error and Exception → RuntimeException.

panels.heading: TRY, CATCH, FINALLY
copy: try contains code that may fail.
catch handles a matching exception.
finally runs after try/catch for cleanup in normal cases.
Do not use a wide catch(Exception) unless that boundary can handle it properly.

panels.heading: GOOD ERROR HANDLING
copy: Catch an exception only when you can recover, add useful context, or translate it.
Keep the original cause when creating another exception.
Never ignore an exception with an empty catch block.
Do not show stack traces or database details to API users.

pages.flowchart: Normal work → problem thrown → matching catch → continue or return safe error.
important: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; unchecked exceptions do not have that compiler rule.
Exceptions should not be used as normal loop or decision logic.
summary: Exceptions describe failed program flow.
Handle them at a place that can make a useful decision.
interview_checks: What is the job of try, catch, and finally?

pages.title: CUSTOM EXCEPTIONS + RESOURCE SAFETY
pages.objective: A custom exception gives a failure a clear application meaning. Try-with-resources closes resources automatically.
pages.layout: Left exception translation ladder; right resource lifecycle.

panels.heading: CUSTOM EXCEPTION
copy: Create one when the failure has a useful domain meaning such as OrderNotFound.
Give it a clear name and useful safe information.
Pass the original exception as the cause when translating a lower-level failure.
Do not create a different exception class for every tiny message.
panels.visual: Database error → OrderLoadException → safe API response.

panels.heading: TRY-WITH-RESOURCES
copy: Files, streams, and database resources must be closed.
A resource implementing AutoCloseable can be declared inside try(...).
Java closes resources automatically, even when work throws an exception.
Resources close in reverse order of creation.

pages.flowchart: Open resource → use resource → success or exception → automatic close.
important: Garbage collection does not replace closing files and database connections.
Public error messages must not expose secrets or internal system details.
summary: Custom exceptions give failures clear meaning.
Try-with-resources makes cleanup reliable.
interview_checks: Why is try-with-resources safer than manually closing a file?

pages.title: GENERICS — TYPE-SAFE REUSABLE CODE
pages.objective: Generics let one class or method work with different types while the compiler still checks type safety.
pages.layout: Before/after boxes and type parameter anatomy.

panels.heading: WHY GENERICS?
copy: Without generics, an Object container needs casts and may fail at runtime.
With Box<String>, the compiler knows only String values belong there.
A type parameter such as T is a placeholder for a real type.
Generics make collections and reusable APIs safer.
panels.visual: Object box with unsafe cast versus Box<String> with compiler check.

panels.heading: COMMON FORMS
copy: Class: Box<T>.
Two types: Map<K,V> for key and value.
Method: <T> T first(List<T> items).
Bound: <T extends Number> accepts Number subtypes.

panels.heading: IMPORTANT LIMIT
copy: List<Integer> is not a child of List<Number>.
Most generic type details are removed at runtime; this is called type erasure.
Primitive types cannot be type arguments; use wrappers such as Integer.

pages.flowchart: Write generic T once → use as String, Integer, Order, and other reference types.
important: Avoid raw List or Box because it removes useful compiler checks.
Use clear type names such as T, K, V, or descriptive names in complex code.
summary: Generics provide reusable code with type safety.
The compiler catches many wrong-type mistakes early.
interview_checks: What problem does Box<T> solve compared with storing Object?

pages.title: WILDCARDS + PECS
pages.objective: A wildcard ? means an unknown type. It helps a method accept a safe family of generic types.
pages.layout: Producer/consumer two-column table with arrows and small examples.

panels.heading: ? extends — PRODUCER
copy: List<? extends Number> means a list of some Number subtype.
We can safely read its items as Number.
We cannot safely add an Integer because the real list might be List<Double>.
Remember: a producer gives values to us.
panels.visual: List<Integer>/List<Double> arrows into read Number.

panels.heading: ? super — CONSUMER
copy: List<? super Integer> means a list that can receive Integer values.
We may add an Integer safely.
When reading, only Object is guaranteed.
Remember: a consumer accepts values from us.

panels.heading: PECS RULE
copy: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.
Use exact List<T> when the method both reads and writes T.
Use a named T when parameter and return types must be connected.

pages.flowchart: Only read T? → extends. Only add T? → super. Read and add T? → exact type.
important: Wildcards are mainly useful in method/API boundaries.
Do not return complicated wildcard types unless callers truly need them.
summary: extends is good for reading.
super is good for adding.
interview_checks: Explain PECS in one sentence.

pages.title: COLLECTIONS FRAMEWORK OVERVIEW
pages.objective: A collection stores and organizes a group of objects. Different collection types provide different rules.
pages.layout: Large hierarchy tree and four-question choice guide.

panels.heading: MAIN INTERFACES
copy: List keeps item positions and allows duplicates.
Set keeps unique items.
Queue keeps items waiting to be processed.
Deque works at both ends and can act as queue or stack.
Map stores key-value pairs and is not a child of Collection.
panels.visual: Iterable → Collection → List/Set/Queue → Deque; separate Map branch.

panels.heading: CHOOSE BY NEED
copy: Need position/order and duplicates? List.
Need uniqueness? Set.
Need lookup by key? Map.
Need first/next work item? Queue.
Need sorted data? Choose a sorted implementation such as TreeSet/TreeMap.

panels.heading: INTERFACE + IMPLEMENTATION
copy: Declare the general interface when possible: List<String>.
Choose an implementation for behavior: new ArrayList<>().
Most normal collections are not safe for changing from many threads at once.

pages.flowchart: What rule do the items need? → List / Set / Queue / Map → choose implementation.
important: Collections store objects, so primitives use wrappers.
Ordering, uniqueness, and thread safety are part of correctness.
summary: Collection type describes the rule for stored items.
Choose by behavior, not habit.
interview_checks: When would you choose Set instead of List?

pages.title: LIST, SET, QUEUE + DEQUE
pages.objective: List, Set, Queue, and Deque are collection interfaces made for different ways of storing and reading items.
pages.layout: Four reference-style rows: meaning, implementations, example, caution.

panels.heading: LIST
copy: ArrayList uses a resizable array and is the common general choice.
It gives fast index access; middle insert/remove may shift items.
LinkedList uses linked nodes and has slow index access.
panels.visual: Array boxes with index numbers.

panels.heading: SET
copy: HashSet gives expected fast membership checks and no sorted order.
LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order.
TreeSet keeps sorted order.
Uniqueness depends on equals and hashCode (or comparison for sorted sets).

panels.heading: QUEUE + DEQUE
copy: Queue normally processes the next item first.
offer adds, poll removes, and peek reads the head without removing.
ArrayDeque is a good normal queue/stack implementation.
PriorityQueue returns the highest-priority head, not fully sorted iteration.

pages.flowchart: Items → need position? List; unique? Set; processing order? Queue/Deque.
important: ArrayList is often faster than LinkedList in real programs because arrays use memory efficiently.
Do not depend on HashSet iteration order.
summary: List = position; Set = unique; Queue = next item.
Implementation decides ordering and speed.
interview_checks: What do offer, poll, and peek do?

pages.title: Map + HashMap INTERNALS
pages.objective: A Map stores a value under a unique key. HashMap uses a key's hashCode and equals methods to find its entry.
pages.layout: Top map picture. Middle put/get flow. Bottom implementation comparison.

panels.heading: MAP BASICS
copy: put(key,value) adds or replaces a value.
get(key) returns the matching value or null when none is found.
containsKey checks whether a key exists.
Keys are unique; different keys may point to equal values.
panels.visual: ID keys on left point to Customer values on right.

panels.heading: HOW HashMap FINDS A KEY
copy: 1. Call key.hashCode().
2. Use the hash to choose a bucket.
3. Check equals among keys in that bucket.
4. Return/replace/add the matching entry.
Different keys may have the same hash; this is called a collision.
panels.visual: Bucket array with two keys in one bucket.

panels.heading: OTHER MAPS
copy: LinkedHashMap keeps insertion or configured access order.
TreeMap keeps keys sorted.
ConcurrentHashMap supports safe concurrent operations and does not allow null keys/values.

pages.flowchart: Key → hashCode → bucket → equals check → value.
important: Do not change fields used by a key's equals/hashCode while it is in the map.
HashMap allows one null key, but using null often makes code less clear.
summary: Map connects keys to values.
hashCode narrows the search; equals confirms the key.
interview_checks: What happens when two different keys have the same hash code?

pages.title: Comparable vs Comparator
pages.objective: Comparable defines a type's natural order. Comparator defines a separate chosen order.
pages.layout: Two-column comparison table and sorting examples.

panels.heading: COMPARABLE
copy: The class implements Comparable<T>.
It defines compareTo(T other).
It is used for one main natural order.
Example: sort Product naturally by product code.
panels.visual: Class owns one natural-order arrow.

panels.heading: COMPARATOR
copy: It is a separate object/function.
It defines compare(a,b).
A type can have many comparators.
Example: sort Product by price, name, or newest date.

panels.heading: RETURN VALUE
copy: Negative means first value comes before second.
Zero means equal in this ordering.
Positive means first comes after second.
Use Comparator.comparing instead of subtracting numbers, which can overflow.

pages.flowchart: Need one natural order? → Comparable. Need a situation-specific order? → Comparator.
important: TreeSet and TreeMap use comparison to decide sorted uniqueness.
Comparator can be reversed and chained with thenComparing.
summary: Comparable lives in the class.
Comparator supplies one outside ordering.
interview_checks: How can the same products be sorted by both name and price?

pages.title: LAMBDAS + FUNCTIONAL INTERFACES
pages.objective: A lambda is a short way to provide a piece of behavior. A functional interface is an interface with one abstract method.
pages.layout: Anonymous class to lambda transformation; four-interface table below.

panels.heading: FROM LONG TO SHORT
copy: Before lambdas, a small behavior often needed an anonymous class.
A lambda writes parameters, an arrow ->, and the action.
The lambda receives its meaning from a functional interface type.
Use @FunctionalInterface to clearly mark the intended contract.
panels.visual: Long anonymous class shrinks into (x) -> action.

panels.heading: COMMON INTERFACES
copy: Predicate<T>: takes T and returns true/false.
Function<T,R>: changes T into R.
Consumer<T>: accepts T and returns nothing.
Supplier<T>: takes nothing and returns T.
panels.visual: Table Interface | Shape | Method | Easy example.

panels.heading: METHOD REFERENCE
copy: A method reference is a shorter lambda that calls an existing method.
name -> print(name) can become System.out::println.
Keep lambdas short; move larger logic to a named method.

pages.flowchart: Input → lambda behavior → output; target interface explains input/output types.
important: A lambda may use a local variable only when it is final or effectively final.
Do not hide large business logic inside one long lambda.
summary: Lambda passes behavior as a value.
Functional interfaces give lambdas a clear type.
interview_checks: What are Predicate and Function used for?

pages.title: STREAM API — FILTER, MAP + COLLECT
pages.objective: A stream is a pipeline that reads data from a source, transforms it, and produces a result.
pages.layout: Large conveyor-belt pipeline with intermediate/terminal table.

panels.heading: STREAM PIPELINE
copy: Source: a collection, array, or other data source.
filter keeps items that match a condition.
map changes each item into another value.
sorted orders items; distinct removes duplicates.
A terminal operation such as toList, count, or collect produces the result.
panels.visual: Orders → filter paid → map IDs → sorted → list.

panels.heading: LAZY WORK
copy: Intermediate operations are lazy: they wait until a terminal operation starts.
A stream is normally used once.
A stream does not store the items; the source stores them.
Avoid changing shared outside data inside a stream operation.

panels.heading: USEFUL OPERATIONS
copy: anyMatch asks whether any item matches.
findFirst returns an Optional result.
flatMap opens and combines nested groups.
groupingBy groups items using a selected value.

code:
List<String> names = users.stream()
    .filter(User::isActive)
    .map(User::getName)
    .sorted()
    .toList();
pages.flowchart: Collection → filter → map → sort → terminal result.
important: Use a normal loop when it is clearer than a stream.
Parallel streams are not automatically faster and are poor for ordinary blocking database/API calls.
summary: Streams describe a data-processing pipeline.
Intermediate steps are lazy; a terminal step starts the work.
interview_checks: What is the difference between filter and map?

pages.title: Optional + DATE/TIME API
pages.objective: Optional represents a result that may be present or absent. java.time classes represent dates and time clearly.
pages.layout: Left Optional railway; right time-type choice table.

panels.heading: OPTIONAL
copy: Optional.of(value) holds a non-null value.
Optional.empty() represents no value.
Use map, orElseGet, and orElseThrow instead of immediately calling get().
It is most useful as a method return type when absence is normal.
panels.visual: Present track → map; empty track → fallback/throw.

panels.heading: TIME TYPES
copy: LocalDate: a date such as 2026-09-27.
LocalTime: time of day without a date.
LocalDateTime: date and time but no zone/offset.
Instant: one exact moment on the global timeline.
ZonedDateTime: date/time with time-zone rules.
Duration measures time; Period measures calendar dates.
panels.visual: Type | Contains | Easy use table.

panels.heading: TESTABLE TIME
copy: Use Clock as a dependency when code needs the current time.
Store global event times as Instant/UTC in many backend systems.
Convert to a user's zone when displaying time.

pages.flowchart: Could result be absent? → Optional return. Need exact event moment? → Instant. Human calendar date? → LocalDate.
important: orElse creates its fallback immediately; orElseGet creates it only when needed.
LocalDateTime alone does not identify one global moment.
summary: Optional clearly shows possible absence.
Choose a time type that contains the information you need.
interview_checks: What is the difference between Instant and LocalDateTime?

pages.title: FILES + INPUT/OUTPUT STREAMS
pages.objective: Input means reading data; output means writing data. Java streams move bytes or characters between a program and another place.
pages.layout: Byte/character comparison and file read/write lifecycle.

panels.heading: BYTE vs CHARACTER
copy: InputStream and OutputStream work with raw bytes, useful for images and binary files.
Reader and Writer work with characters, useful for text.
Buffered versions reduce expensive small read/write operations.
Files utility methods provide simple operations for paths and small files.
panels.visual: Binary file → byte stream; text file → reader/writer.

panels.heading: PATH + FILES
copy: Path represents a file-system path.
Files.exists checks existence.
Files.readString/writeString are convenient for small text files.
Large files should be streamed instead of fully loaded into memory.

panels.heading: SAFE USE
copy: Use try-with-resources so open files close.
Choose the correct character encoding, commonly UTF-8.
Validate file names/paths when they come from users to prevent path traversal.

pages.flowchart: Path → open → read/write in chunks → close automatically.
important: A file is outside Java heap memory, but loaded file contents use heap memory.
Never trust a user-provided file path without validation.
summary: Byte streams handle binary; character streams handle text.
Close resources and choose encoding explicitly.
interview_checks: When would you use Reader instead of InputStream?

pages.title: THREADS + CONCURRENCY BASICS
pages.objective: A thread is one path of work inside a program. Concurrency means several tasks can make progress during the same time period.
pages.layout: Thread lifecycle on top; race-condition timeline below.

panels.heading: WHY THREADS?
copy: A server handles many user requests, often using many threads.
Concurrency can improve responsiveness and throughput.
More threads do not always mean more speed; CPU and other resources are limited.
Call start() to begin a new thread; directly calling run() is a normal method call.
panels.visual: Thread states: NEW → RUNNABLE → WAITING/BLOCKED → TERMINATED.

panels.heading: RACE CONDITION
copy: A race happens when threads read/write shared data without safe coordination.
count++ is read, add, and write—not one guaranteed atomic step.
Two threads may both read 10 and both write 11, losing one update.
Prefer immutable/local data before adding locks.
panels.visual: Two-thread timeline showing lost update.

panels.heading: SAFE TOOLS
copy: synchronized allows one thread at a time in a protected section and makes changes visible.
volatile helps visibility for one variable but does not make count++ atomic.
AtomicInteger provides atomic operations for a single integer value.

pages.flowchart: Shared mutable data? → avoid sharing if possible → otherwise choose atomic value or protected critical section.
important: sleep pauses a thread but does not release a lock it holds.
Interruption is a cooperative request for a thread to stop/wake, not a forced kill.
summary: Threads allow concurrent work.
Shared changing data needs a safety plan.
interview_checks: Why is volatile not enough for count++?

pages.title: EXECUTORS + CompletableFuture
pages.objective: An Executor manages worker threads for us. CompletableFuture represents work that may finish later.
pages.layout: Executor queue diagram and future composition railway.

panels.heading: EXECUTOR
copy: Submit a Runnable when no result is needed.
Submit a Callable<T> when a result is needed.
A thread pool reuses a limited number of worker threads.
A bounded queue prevents unlimited waiting tasks from filling memory.
Shut down an executor when its owner stops.
panels.visual: Tasks → bounded queue → worker threads → results.

panels.heading: CompletableFuture
copy: supplyAsync starts work that returns a value.
thenApply changes a completed value.
thenCompose starts a next async step and avoids a nested future.
thenCombine joins independent results.
exceptionally can provide a fallback for a failure.

panels.heading: LIMITS
copy: Always use timeouts for remote work.
Choose an intentional executor for blocking work.
Async code does not make a slow database faster.
Modern virtual threads make many blocking tasks cheaper, but downstream limits still matter.

pages.flowchart: Submit task → queue → worker executes → future completes → next step or error path.
important: A very large pool can overload the database or another service.
thenApply maps a value; thenCompose connects another future.
summary: Executors control thread resources.
CompletableFuture connects work that finishes later.
interview_checks: What is the difference between thenApply and thenCompose?

pages.title: JVM MEMORY + GARBAGE COLLECTION
pages.objective: The JVM uses several memory areas. Garbage collection automatically frees heap objects that are no longer reachable.
pages.layout: Large labeled memory map and reachable-object drawing.

panels.heading: MEMORY AREAS
copy: Heap: most objects and arrays; shared by threads.
Stack: each thread's method calls and local working values.
Metaspace: class information in native memory.
Code cache: machine code created by the JIT compiler.
Direct/native memory: buffers, thread stacks, and native libraries outside the heap.
panels.visual: One process split into heap, per-thread stacks, metaspace, code cache, native.

panels.heading: GARBAGE COLLECTION
copy: GC starts from roots such as active thread stacks and static references.
Objects reachable from roots stay alive.
Unreachable objects may be collected.
GC manages memory, but it does not close files or database connections for us.
panels.visual: Green reachable graph and faded unreachable island.

panels.heading: COMMON PROBLEMS
copy: StackOverflowError often comes from endless/deep recursion.
OutOfMemoryError means a memory area could not provide more space.
An unbounded cache or list can keep unwanted objects reachable.
Use measurements, GC logs, thread dumps, heap dumps, and Java Flight Recorder to investigate.

pages.flowchart: Create object → reachable while used → no path from roots → eligible for collection.
important: A Java memory leak means unwanted objects are still reachable.
Do not call System.gc() as a normal fix.
summary: Heap stores objects; stacks hold thread method work.
GC removes unreachable objects.
interview_checks: Can Java have a memory leak even with garbage collection?

pages.title: SOLID PRINCIPLES — EASY VERSION
pages.objective: SOLID is a set of five design ideas that help code stay understandable and easier to change.
pages.layout: Five reference-style rows with simple definition and example.

panels.heading: S — SINGLE RESPONSIBILITY
copy: A class should have one main reason to change.
OrderService should not also generate PDFs and send every email.
panels.visual: Large mixed class splits into focused helpers.

panels.heading: O — OPEN/CLOSED
copy: Add a new behavior with a safe extension instead of repeatedly changing stable code.
PaymentStrategy can gain a new payment type.

panels.heading: L — LISKOV SUBSTITUTION
copy: A child implementation must keep the promise of its parent type.
A subtype should not surprise callers by rejecting valid parent operations.

panels.heading: I — INTERFACE SEGREGATION
copy: Prefer small useful interfaces over one huge interface.
A reader should not be forced to implement write methods.

panels.heading: D — DEPENDENCY INVERSION
copy: Business code depends on a useful contract, not directly on vendor/database details.
CheckoutService depends on PaymentGateway.

pages.flowchart: Find responsibility → find change point → create smallest clear boundary → test the behavior.
important: SOLID is guidance, not a rule to create the maximum number of classes.
Create an abstraction only when it makes the design clearer.
summary: SOLID helps separate responsibilities and changes.
Simple code is more important than blindly following a pattern.
interview_checks: Explain one SOLID principle with a simple example.

pages.title: COMMON DESIGN PATTERNS
pages.objective: A design pattern is a common way to solve a problem that appears again and again in software.
pages.layout: Four pattern cards with problem, shape, and backend example.

panels.heading: FACTORY
copy: Problem: the program must choose which object to create.
Factory keeps creation/selection in one place.
Example: NotificationFactory returns EmailSender or SmsSender.
panels.visual: Input type → Factory → chosen object.

panels.heading: BUILDER
copy: Problem: an object has many optional construction values.
Builder names each value and creates the final object.
Example: building an HTTP request or test data.

panels.heading: STRATEGY
copy: Problem: one task has several interchangeable ways.
Each strategy follows one contract.
Example: CardPayment and UpiPayment implement PaymentStrategy.

panels.heading: ADAPTER + DECORATOR
copy: Adapter changes an external API into the interface our app expects.
Decorator wraps an object to add logging, caching, metrics, or retry.
Spring often uses proxies with decorator-like behavior.

code:
PaymentStrategy strategy = strategies.get(type);
PaymentResult result = strategy.pay(command);
pages.flowchart: Repeated design problem → understand trade-offs → choose smallest useful pattern → keep code readable.
important: Patterns are names for solutions, not goals by themselves.
Singleton means one instance in a particular container/context, not one object in the whole distributed system.
summary: Patterns give developers a shared design language.
Use one only when it makes the problem simpler.
interview_checks: What problem does the Strategy pattern solve?

pages.title: MAVEN, PROJECT STRUCTURE + GIT
pages.objective: Maven builds Java projects and manages libraries. Git records code changes and helps a team work together.
pages.layout: Maven lifecycle at top, project tree and Git flow below.

panels.heading: MAVEN
copy: pom.xml describes the project, dependencies, plugins, and settings.
A dependency is a library the code uses.
A plugin performs build work.
Common flow: validate → compile → test → package → verify → install.
Maven Wrapper (mvnw) helps a team use the intended Maven version.
panels.visual: Long lifecycle arrow.

panels.heading: PROJECT STRUCTURE
copy: src/main/java contains application Java code.
src/main/resources contains configuration/templates/static resources.
src/test/java contains tests.
target contains generated build output and should not be committed.
Grouping code by business feature often keeps related work together.

panels.heading: GIT FLOW
copy: Create a small branch/change, make focused commits, and open a pull request.
Automated checks and review run before merging.
Never commit passwords, secret keys, target output, or personal IDE files.

code:
./mvnw clean verify
./mvnw spring-boot:run
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Add order validation"
pages.flowchart: Source + pom.xml → compile → test → package JAR → deploy; Git commit → review → main.
important: Use dependency:tree to understand library version conflicts.
A secret remains in old Git history even after deleting it from the latest file.
summary: Maven makes builds repeatable.
Git records and reviews code changes.
interview_checks: What is the difference between a Maven dependency and plugin?

pages.title: HTTP, URL + JSON BASICS
pages.objective: HTTP is the request-response language used by web clients and servers. JSON is a common text format for request and response data.
pages.layout: Large HTTP request/response cards and method table.

panels.heading: HTTP REQUEST
copy: Method says the action: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE.
URL identifies the address/resource.
Headers carry extra information such as content type or authorization.
Body carries data when needed, often JSON.
panels.visual: Request card with method, path, headers, body labels.

panels.heading: HTTP RESPONSE
copy: Status code explains the result.
Headers describe the response.
Body carries returned data or an error.
Common codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error.

panels.heading: JSON
copy: JSON objects use { } and name-value pairs.
JSON arrays use [ ].
Strings use double quotes.
JSON has no comments and does not know Java class types by itself.

pages.flowchart: Client builds HTTP request → server processes → server sends status + headers + optional JSON.
important: HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS encryption in transit.
A 401 means authentication is needed/failed; 403 means the known user is not allowed.
summary: HTTP carries requests and responses.
JSON carries structured text data.
interview_checks: What are the four main parts of an HTTP request?

pages.title: DATABASE + SQL CRUD
pages.objective: A relational database stores information in tables. SQL is the language used to create, read, update, and delete that information.
pages.layout: Table anatomy on top; CRUD four-row examples below.

panels.heading: TABLE BASICS
copy: A table represents one kind of information, such as customers.
A row represents one record.
A column represents one property and has a data type.
A primary key uniquely identifies a row.
A foreign key links a row to another table.
panels.visual: Customer table with row, column, primary key labels.

panels.heading: CRUD
copy: CREATE data: INSERT.
READ data: SELECT.
UPDATE data: UPDATE.
DELETE data: DELETE.
WHERE chooses which rows are affected.

panels.heading: SAFE VALUES
copy: Use SQL parameters instead of joining user input into SQL text.
Database constraints such as NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and FOREIGN KEY protect valid data.
Application validation gives friendly errors; database constraints protect every writer.

pages.flowchart: Application sends parameterized SQL → database checks constraints → rows change/result returns.
important: UPDATE or DELETE without the intended WHERE can affect every row.
NULL means missing/unknown; check it with IS NULL, not = NULL.
summary: Tables contain rows and columns.
CRUD means create, read, update, and delete.
interview_checks: What is the purpose of a primary key and foreign key?

pages.title: SQL FILTERING, GROUPING + JOINS
pages.objective: Filtering chooses rows, grouping summarizes rows, and joins combine related rows from tables.
pages.layout: Top logical query order. Middle joins drawing. Bottom aggregate example.

panels.heading: FILTER + GROUP
copy: WHERE filters individual rows.
GROUP BY places matching values into groups.
COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX summarize data.
HAVING filters completed groups.
ORDER BY sorts the final result.
panels.visual: Rows → WHERE → groups → HAVING → ordered result.

panels.heading: JOINS
copy: INNER JOIN returns rows with a match on both sides.
LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and uses NULL where no right match exists.
The ON condition explains how rows are related.
Joining one-to-many data can produce several result rows for one parent.
panels.visual: Customers and Orders key rows connected; show inner/left results.

panels.heading: LOGICAL ORDER
copy: FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
Knowing this order explains why a selected alias may not be usable in WHERE.

code:
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM customer c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.active = TRUE
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(o.id) >= 2
ORDER BY order_count DESC;
pages.flowchart: Choose tables → join → filter rows → group → filter groups → select → sort.
important: A condition on the right table in WHERE can accidentally remove unmatched LEFT JOIN rows.
Select only the columns the application needs.
summary: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.
Joins combine related table data.
interview_checks: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?

pages.title: INDEXES + ACID TRANSACTIONS
pages.objective: An index helps a database find rows faster. A transaction groups database work into one reliable unit.
pages.layout: B-tree picture on left; ACID four-box diagram and transfer flow on right.

panels.heading: DATABASE INDEX
copy: An index is an extra ordered structure built from selected columns.
It can speed up filtering, joining, and sorting.
It uses storage and makes inserts/updates/deletes do extra work.
A composite index contains more than one column; column order matters.
Use the database query plan to check whether an index helps.
panels.visual: Book index analogy and small B-tree.

panels.heading: ACID
copy: Atomicity: all transaction steps succeed or all are undone.
Consistency: constraints/rules remain valid.
Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see unsafe partial work.
Durability: committed data survives expected failures.
panels.visual: Four boxes around money transfer.

panels.heading: ISOLATION IDEA
copy: Concurrent users may read/change the same rows.
Isolation levels choose which changes can be seen and what conflicts may happen.
Keep transactions short so locks and database connections are not held too long.

pages.flowchart: Begin → perform related SQL → success? commit : rollback.
important: More indexes are not always better; they cost space and write time.
A transaction does not automatically include a remote API or message broker.
summary: Indexes trade write/storage cost for faster reads.
Transactions protect a group of database changes.
interview_checks: What does Atomicity mean in a bank transfer?

pages.title: JDBC + CONNECTION POOL
pages.objective: JDBC is Java's basic API for talking to relational databases. A connection pool reuses a limited set of database connections.
pages.layout: JDBC sequence on top; pool checkout/return below.

panels.heading: JDBC PARTS
copy: DataSource provides database connections.
Connection represents one database session.
PreparedStatement holds parameterized SQL.
ResultSet lets code read returned rows.
SQLException describes a database-access failure.
panels.visual: Java → DataSource → Connection → PreparedStatement → DB → ResultSet.

panels.heading: PREPARED STATEMENT
copy: SQL structure and input values are kept separate.
This is the normal defense against SQL injection for values.
Each ? placeholder receives a typed value.
Close Connection, Statement, and ResultSet with try-with-resources.

panels.heading: CONNECTION POOL
copy: Opening a physical connection is expensive, so a pool reuses connections.
A request borrows a connection and closing it returns it to the pool.
Pool size is limited because the database has limited capacity.
Slow queries/long transactions can exhaust the pool.

pages.flowchart: Borrow connection → prepare/bind → execute → read result → close returns connection.
important: Never build SQL by directly joining untrusted input into the query.
A larger connection pool can overload the database instead of fixing slow SQL.
summary: JDBC sends safe SQL and reads results.
A pool treats connections as limited reusable resources.
interview_checks: Why should JDBC code use PreparedStatement?

pages.title: JPA + HIBERNATE BASICS
pages.objective: JPA is a Java standard for mapping objects to relational data. Hibernate is a common tool that implements JPA.
pages.layout: Object/table mapping picture and entity lifecycle below.

panels.heading: ORM IDEA
copy: ORM means Object-Relational Mapping.
A Java entity class maps to a database table.
An entity object maps to a row; fields map to columns.
JPA defines annotations/APIs; Hibernate performs the work.
JPA saves boilerplate but does not remove the need to understand SQL.
panels.visual: Order object fields align with orders table columns.

panels.heading: ENTITY BASICS
copy: @Entity marks a persistent class.
@Id marks its identity/primary key.
@GeneratedValue asks a configured strategy to create an ID.
Entities need an accessible no-argument constructor for JPA.
Use a transaction when changing stored data.

panels.heading: ENTITY STATES
copy: Transient: new object not managed/saved.
Managed: tracked by the persistence context.
Detached: no longer tracked.
Removed: marked for deletion.
Dirty checking writes changes made to managed entities.
panels.visual: State circles with persist, detach, remove arrows.

pages.flowchart: Entity object → EntityManager/Hibernate → generated SQL → database row.
important: Do not expose JPA entities directly as API response objects.
flush sends pending SQL but transaction commit makes it durable.
summary: JPA maps objects and tables.
Hibernate tracks managed entities and executes SQL.
interview_checks: What is the difference between JPA and Hibernate?

pages.title: JPA RELATIONSHIPS, FETCHING + N+1
pages.objective: JPA relationships map links between entities. Fetching decides when related data is loaded.
pages.layout: Relationship symbols on top; N+1 query timeline and fixes below.

panels.heading: RELATIONSHIPS
copy: @OneToOne: one row relates to one row.
@OneToMany: one parent relates to many children.
@ManyToOne: many children point to one parent.
@ManyToMany: many on both sides, usually through a join table.
The owning side controls the foreign key/join mapping.
panels.visual: Customer 1 → many Orders; Order 1 → many LineItems.

panels.heading: LAZY vs EAGER
copy: Lazy means related data loads when it is accessed.
Eager means it is requested with the entity, but exact SQL still matters.
Neither choice is correct for every use case.
Choose a fetch plan for the data one screen/API needs.

panels.heading: N+1 PROBLEM
copy: One query loads N parent rows.
Reading each lazy child list causes up to N more queries.
Fix choices include fetch join, EntityGraph, DTO projection, or batch fetching.
Loading everything eagerly can create another performance problem.
panels.visual: One parent query followed by N red child queries.

panels.heading: CASCADE
copy: Cascade passes operations such as persist/remove from parent to related entities.
orphanRemoval deletes a child removed from an owned collection.
Use both only when object lifecycle ownership is clear.

code:
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = PERSIST)
private List<LineItem> items = new ArrayList<>();
pages.flowchart: API data need → choose projection/fetch plan → run query → count queries and rows.
important: A collection fetch join and pagination can produce wrong/expensive results; often page parent IDs first.
Keep both sides of a bidirectional relationship consistent.
summary: Mappings describe relationships and ownership.
N+1 means one starting query plus many repeated queries.
interview_checks: What is the N+1 problem and one way to fix it?

pages.title: SPRING, IoC + DEPENDENCY INJECTION
pages.objective: Spring is a Java framework that creates and connects application objects. IoC means Spring controls this object setup.
pages.layout: Without/with Spring comparison and constructor injection example.

panels.heading: WITHOUT SPRING
copy: A class directly creates its dependencies using new.
Object setup becomes spread across the application.
Replacing a real dependency with a test version becomes harder.
panels.visual: OrderService → new OrderRepository/new EmailClient.

panels.heading: WITH SPRING IoC
copy: We describe which classes are Spring beans.
ApplicationContext creates the bean objects.
It finds their dependencies and connects them.
It also manages lifecycle and may add proxy behavior.
panels.visual: Container creates Repository and injects it into Service.

panels.heading: CONSTRUCTOR INJECTION
copy: Required dependencies appear in the constructor.
They can be final and are available when the object is created.
A plain unit test can call the constructor directly.
Too many constructor parameters may mean a class has too many jobs.

pages.flowchart: Spring reads configuration/components → creates beans → finds constructor needs → injects dependencies.
important: An object created manually with new is not automatically managed by Spring.
Constructor injection is usually clearer than hidden field injection.
summary: IoC gives object setup to the container.
Dependency injection supplies the objects a class needs.
interview_checks: Why is constructor injection useful?

pages.title: SPRING BEANS + COMMON ANNOTATIONS
pages.objective: A Spring bean is an object created and managed by the Spring container.
pages.layout: Annotation family tree and bean creation flow.

panels.heading: STEREOTYPE ANNOTATIONS
copy: @Component: general Spring-managed component.
@Service: application/business service.
@Repository: data-access component; also supports exception translation.
@Controller: MVC controller that may return views.
@RestController: controller whose methods normally return response bodies such as JSON.
panels.visual: @Component branches to specialized stereotypes.

panels.heading: EXPLICIT BEANS
copy: @Configuration marks a class containing bean configuration.
@Bean marks a method whose returned object becomes a bean.
This is useful for third-party classes we cannot annotate.
A single constructor normally does not need @Autowired.

panels.heading: MULTIPLE BEANS
copy: When two beans match one type, Spring needs help choosing.
@Primary marks the normal choice.
@Qualifier names the intended role.
Injecting a Map<String, Strategy> can support many strategies.

pages.flowchart: Component scan or @Bean → bean definition → object created → dependencies injected → ready.
important: The annotation name communicates purpose but does not automatically make business design correct.
Circular constructor dependencies usually show responsibilities that should be redesigned.
summary: A bean is a container-managed object.
Scanning and @Bean methods register beans.
interview_checks: When would you use @Bean instead of @Component?

pages.title: BEAN LIFECYCLE, SCOPES + PROXIES
pages.objective: Bean lifecycle describes how Spring creates, prepares, uses, and destroys a bean. Scope describes how many bean objects exist.
pages.layout: Lifecycle conveyor, scope table, and proxy wrapper picture.

panels.heading: LIFECYCLE
copy: Spring reads a bean definition.
It creates the object and injects dependencies.
Bean post-processors can inspect or wrap it.
@PostConstruct runs after setup.
The bean is used.
@PreDestroy runs during a normal container shutdown.
panels.visual: Definition → create → inject → initialize → use → destroy.

panels.heading: SCOPES
copy: singleton: one bean per ApplicationContext; the normal scope.
prototype: a new bean when requested from the container.
request: one bean per web request.
session: one bean per web session.
Singleton beans serve many threads, so avoid request-specific mutable fields.
panels.visual: Scope | Lifetime | Simple use table.

panels.heading: PROXY
copy: Spring can return a wrapper called a proxy around a bean.
The proxy adds transactions, security, caching, or async behavior.
A call from a method to another method on this may skip the proxy.
That is why self-invoked @Transactional may not work as expected.
panels.visual: Caller → Proxy → target bean; internal arrow bypasses proxy.

pages.flowchart: Caller → proxy extra behavior → real method → proxy finishes behavior → result.
important: Singleton means one per container, not one in the whole cluster.
Do not start slow work or unmanaged threads inside a bean constructor.
summary: Spring controls bean creation and cleanup.
Proxies add framework behavior around method calls.
interview_checks: Why can self-invocation bypass @Transactional?

pages.title: SPRING BOOT + AUTO-CONFIGURATION
pages.objective: Spring Boot makes Spring applications faster to start by providing useful defaults, dependency starters, and automatic configuration.
pages.layout: @SpringBootApplication branches and conditional decision flow.

panels.heading: WHAT BOOT PROVIDES
copy: Starter dependencies collect common libraries, such as spring-boot-starter-web.
Auto-configuration suggests beans based on libraries, properties, and existing beans.
An embedded server lets a web app run as one executable JAR.
Actuator adds optional production health and metric endpoints.
panels.visual: Spring Boot box: starters, auto-config, server, actuator.

panels.heading: @SpringBootApplication
copy: It includes configuration support.
It starts component scanning from its package downward.
It enables Boot's auto-configuration selection.
Place the main class near the top package so features are scanned.

panels.heading: CONDITIONAL SETUP
copy: Is a required class present?
Is a property enabled?
Did the application already define its own bean?
When a user bean exists, auto-configuration often backs off.
The condition report helps explain why a configuration matched.
panels.visual: Decision diamonds ending Create default bean / Back off.

pages.flowchart: Classpath + properties + user beans → conditions → auto-configured beans → running application.
important: Auto-configuration is conditional setup, not magic.
Do not exclude an auto-configuration before understanding what condition matched.
summary: Boot supplies sensible conditional defaults.
The application can replace defaults when needed.
interview_checks: What three ideas are combined by @SpringBootApplication?

pages.title: CONFIGURATION + PROFILES
pages.objective: Configuration means values that may change between environments without changing the Java code.
pages.layout: One JAR to three environments and typed properties card.

panels.heading: EXTERNAL CONFIG
copy: application.properties or application.yml provides defaults.
Environment variables and command-line values can override configuration.
Use the same built artifact in development, test, and production.
Inject each environment's URLs, limits, and feature values during deployment.
panels.visual: One JAR flows to dev/stage/prod; each supplies config.

panels.heading: PROFILES
copy: A profile activates environment- or purpose-specific configuration/beans.
Example: application-dev.yml.
Profiles may be combined, so test the real combination.
Do not use profiles for every small business feature choice.

panels.heading: TYPED PROPERTIES
copy: @ConfigurationProperties maps a group of values to a typed class/record.
Validation can stop startup when a required value is missing.
This is clearer than many scattered @Value fields.
Secrets belong in a secret manager/platform secret, never Git.

code:
payment:
  base-url: https://api.example.com
  timeout: 2s
pages.flowchart: Config sources → precedence/override → typed binding → validation → bean uses safe values.
important: Never log all environment values because they may contain secrets.
Configuration changes environment behavior; the artifact stays unchanged.
summary: External configuration keeps code and environment values separate.
Typed properties make configuration clear and testable.
interview_checks: Why should production secrets not be stored in application.yml in Git?

pages.title: SPRING MVC REQUEST LIFECYCLE
pages.objective: Spring MVC receives an HTTP request, finds the correct controller method, converts data, and creates an HTTP response.
pages.layout: Full-page numbered request sequence with component notes.

panels.heading: BEFORE CONTROLLER
copy: 1. The embedded server accepts the request.
2. Servlet Filters run for concerns such as security and request IDs.
3. DispatcherServlet acts as Spring MVC's front controller.
4. HandlerMapping finds a matching controller method.
5. Argument resolvers and message converters create method parameters.
panels.visual: Client → Server/Filters → DispatcherServlet → Controller.

panels.heading: CONTROLLER + SERVICE
copy: 6. JSON may be converted into a request DTO.
7. Validation runs when requested.
8. The controller calls an application service.
9. The service applies rules and uses repositories.
10. The controller returns a result or ResponseEntity.

panels.heading: RESPONSE
copy: 11. A message converter changes the response object into JSON.
12. Exception handlers translate known failures into safe error responses.
13. The response passes back through filters to the client.

pages.flowchart: Client → filters → DispatcherServlet → mapping/binding → controller → service → repository → JSON response.
important: Controllers are singleton beans, so do not store one user's request data in controller fields.
Spring MVC normally uses the servlet blocking model; WebFlux is a separate reactive stack.
summary: DispatcherServlet coordinates the MVC request.
Controllers adapt HTTP to application calls.
interview_checks: What happens between incoming JSON and a controller parameter?

pages.title: REST CONTROLLERS + API DESIGN
pages.objective: A REST API exposes resources through HTTP methods, URLs, status codes, headers, and representations such as JSON.
pages.layout: Resource URL examples, HTTP method table, status-code guide.

panels.heading: RESOURCE URLS
copy: Use nouns: /orders and /orders/42.
Avoid action names such as /getOrder when GET already describes the action.
A nested path such as /orders/42/items can show clear ownership.
